articles.title: NFL commissioner Roger Goodell visits Illinois again for more Bears stadium talks with Gov. JB Pritzker
articles.description: Illinois is still moving the chains in stadium talks to keep the Bears from jumping the state line to Indiana, officials said Thursday. Gov. JB Pritzker met with NFL commissioner Roger Goodell, Bears minority owner Pat Ryan and the top legislative leaders who have been wrangling for several years over the property tax incentives the team is seeking to break ground in Arlington Heights. It was Goodell’s second meeting in as many months with Illinois officials, while Ryan — who bankrolled his namesake stadium opening later this week at Northwestern University — takes a more active role in negotiations with the state over Bears president Kevin Warren, who hasn’t made inroads in Springfield. The conversation, held in Chicago, also included Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch and the Capitol’s top stadium negotiators, South Side state Sen. Bill Cunningham and downtown state Rep. Kam Buckner. Pritzker’s office noted they’ve “remained in conversation with the Bears about their plans in Illinois throughout the summer,” since the team announced in June that they were shifting focus to Hammond, Indiana. Sources familiar with Thursday’s discussion suggested there was no major breakthrough, but some optimism that common ground could be found before lawmakers return to Springfield in mid-November for the fall veto session. Further meetings are expected this month. "The Governor and General Assembly leadership were glad to participate in a productive meeting focused on keeping the Bears in Illinois and protecting taxpayers,” Pritzker’s office said in a press release announcing the meeting. "The NFL appreciated the opportunity to meet with Gov. Pritzker and legislative leaders today,” NFL spokesman Brian McCarthy said in a statement. “Timely action is essential as the Bears work to find a long-term stadium solution for the club and their fans." A Bears spokesman didn’t reply to a request for comment. Hoosier lawmakers have rolled out the red carpet for the Bears with legislation that would pump upwards of a billion taxpayer dollars into a new stadium. Earlier this year, the Illinois House passed a bill that would allow the Bears to negotiate a discounted payment in lieu of taxes with local taxing bodies, earning critical support from Chicago Democrats because it would’ve shared proceeds with homeowners as property tax rebates — but those returns were deemed “ negligible .” The Illinois Senate passed a separate bill that would allow municipalities to create their own stadium authorities to negotiate with teams, but it crumbled in the waning hours of spring session without a vote in the other chamber . The Bears turned their noses at both measures, but haven’t spelled out what they want from the state beyond “property tax certainty.” Ryan, a billionaire with a 10% stake in the team, has helped improve the tenor of discussions that had stagnated between Illinois officials and Halas Hall, according to sources familiar with the talks. Goodell has toured the potential stadium sites in Arlington Heights and Hammond. Without stating a preference, he has publicly urged the Bears to come to a resolution “soon” — but Illinois sources are taking his visits as an indication that the league thinks the team is better off in its original state. The Bears have committed to putting $2 billion into a new stadium wherever they end up. They’re under lease at Soldier Field until 2033. Contributing: Sun-Times sports reporter Pat Finley

Sky to bring back coach Tyler Marsh for third season
articles.description: Tyler Marsh has new life. Just a week ago he was reckoning with his future in Chicago after another season failed to live up to expectations. He told reporters that whether or not he was back leading the Sky in 2027, he was grateful for his experience — and that he if he was back, he'd approach it with the same zeal he always has. Now he can rest easy. The Sky front office wants to see what the third-year coach can do, confirming that he’ll be returning next season. “It was going to be incredibly unfair to judge someone that has yet to play with healthy rosters as a young coach,” general manager Jeff Pagliocca said in his exit interview on Thursday. Marsh’s luck hasn’t been great since joining the Sky as a first-time head coach in 2025. In each year one of his top players tore their ACL — Courtney Vandersloot in 2025 and Rickea Jackson in 2026. This season he also started the year without Vandersloot and Azura Stevens, and ultimately lost point guard Skylar Diggins to injury 19 games in. Still, midway through the season, Pagliocca told the Sun-Times that even despite the injuries across their starting lineup, he expected the team to make the playoffs. The Sky finished well short in 11th place, and blowing close games was a big reason why. Pagliocca said Thursday that he saw enough growth from Marsh to give him confidence. “I never heard him make excuses," Pagliocca said of Marsh. "I never heard him shy away from taking responsibility, in a lot of moments where he didn’t need to or shouldn’t have. We were in those games. Whether the players weren't executing or he wasn’t executing, he was owning that responsibility. "He’s as selfless as I’ve been around. He coaches for the right reasons. He kept the locker room intact. “He knows what he wants to do differently, and he’s made me believe that he’s the guy to lead this team."
